article.headline: A Classic Recession Gauge Matches Its 2008 Low — With Caveats
article.lede: The ratio of forward-looking to real-time economic signals has touched a level last seen at the nadir of the 2008 financial crisis, reviving a debate the American economy seemed to have settled two years ago. The *Leading Economic Index-to-Coincident Economic Index* ratio compiled by The Conference Board fell to 0.84 in March 2026, as the *LEI* declined for the seventh time in eight months. The *CEI* — tracking payrolls, personal income, industrial output, and trade sales — held flat, widening the gap between what the data anticipates and what it currently observes.
article.body:
The **Leading Economic Index** (*LEI*) is an average of ten data series chosen for their tendency to turn before the broader economy does: building permits, manufacturing orders, initial jobless claims, equity prices, credit conditions, and the yield spread between ten-year Treasuries and the federal funds rate, among others. The **Coincident Economic Index** (*CEI*) measures what is happening now — nonfarm payrolls, personal income excluding government transfers, industrial production, and manufacturing and trade sales. Their ratio, derived by dividing one into the other, is a compact read on how sharply forward-looking signals have diverged from current conditions. At 0.84 in March 2026, the ratio sits at a level the historical record dating to 1960 associates exclusively with formal recessions.

The trouble is the immediate history that record is up against. Between mid-2022 and late 2024, the LEI fell for roughly 22 consecutive months — nearly matching the 24-month streak during the Global Financial Crisis — while real GDP grew at close to 3% annualized. The Conference Board issued and then successively retreated from six recession forecasts, each targeting a quarter that came and went without contraction. The structural reason is a known flaw: the LEI's components weight manufacturing and business sentiment at roughly 44% of the index, while consumption accounts for approximately 68% of actual GDP. The index was calibrated for an economy that no longer quite exists. Ed Yardeni of Yardeni Research — whose firm's LEI/CEI ratio chart is cited as the data source for the tweet — has called the measure "long overdue for a product recall," a pointed observation given that his chart is now being presented as recession evidence.

The Conference Board's own formal threshold — the **"3Ds" rule**, requiring sufficient *Duration*, *Depth*, and *Diffusion* across components before a recession call — has not been formally crossed by the March 2026 data. The six-month rate of LEI decline is -1.0%, decelerating from -2.1% in the prior six months; the deterioration is stabilizing in pace, if not reversing. The Conference Board's own GDP forecast for 2026 stands at 1.6% growth, below potential but positive.

What is harder to dismiss is the changed backdrop. The false-signal years of 2022–2024 unfolded against extraordinary fiscal stimulus and pandemic-era distortions in consumer balance sheets that the LEI's components could not adequately capture. The Conference Board's March 2026 release explicitly cites higher oil prices and supply-chain disruptions — products of renewed tariffs — as forces compressing consumer purchasing power in real time. If a shock is what converts a recession signal into a recession, the macro landscape currently offers several candidates. The divergence between what forward indicators signal and what payrolls currently show must close in one direction eventually. History offers examples of both outcomes.

concepts.definition: A composite of ten forward-looking data series — including building permits, manufacturing orders, initial jobless claims, stock prices, and the Treasury yield spread — designed to signal turning points in the economy before they appear in current data. Published monthly by The Conference Board. It tends to peak and trough before aggregate economic activity does, though its predictive reliability has been questioned in post-COVID cycles.

A composite of four real-time economic measures — nonfarm payrolls, personal income excluding government transfers, industrial production, and manufacturing and trade sales — that move broadly in step with the current state of the economy. Produced by The Conference Board alongside the LEI. Unlike the LEI, the CEI reflects what is happening now rather than what is anticipated.

The Leading Economic Index divided by the Coincident Economic Index, used as a shorthand for how sharply forward-looking signals have diverged from current conditions. A falling ratio means the economy's warning gauges are deteriorating faster than its real-time readings, which has historically preceded recessions. The ratio is a market convention, not an official Conference Board product.

The Conference Board's formal internal framework for calling a recession from LEI data, requiring three conditions to be met simultaneously: sufficient Duration (a sustained period of decline), Depth (the magnitude of the index's fall), and Diffusion (the breadth of decline across individual components, measured by a six-month diffusion index falling at or below 50). Meeting all three thresholds is a higher bar than a simple string of monthly declines.

In this context, the difference between the ten-year US Treasury yield and the federal funds rate. A positive spread (long rates above short rates) is the norm and signals confidence in growth; an inverted spread (short rates above long rates) has historically preceded recessions, which is why it is one of the LEI's ten components. Extended inversions in 2022–2024 contributed to the LEI's false recession signals.

A measure of how broadly a decline or advance is spread across components of a composite index. For the LEI, the six-month diffusion index tracks what share of the ten components are rising versus falling over a half-year window. A reading at or below 50 — meaning more components are falling than rising — is one leg of the Conference Board's 3Ds recession threshold.

article.fact_check: The claim that such depressed LEI/CEI ratios have 'never occurred outside of a recession' is approximately valid for the 0.84 level based on the historical record back to 1960, and the comparison to the 2008 Financial Crisis low is directionally accurate (LEI 97.3 ÷ CEI 115.2 ≈ 0.845). However, the claim requires significant context: the LEI declined for roughly 22 consecutive months across 2022–2024 without a recession materializing — the longest such false-signal streak in modern memory. The assertion that the ratio is on track for its 'fifth consecutive annual decline, the longest streak on record' is plausible given that LEI peaked in December 2021 and has trended down through each subsequent calendar year, but this specific claim could not be independently verified against primary Conference Board historical data tables during this research. The broader framing — 'in the past, such depressed levels have never occurred outside of a recession' — is also complicated by the post-COVID period, in which the LEI reached analogously stressed readings while GDP grew at near-trend rates.
